entries.meaning: I bow to the pollen-like dust of my teacher’s lotus feet: beautiful, fragrant, nectar-rich and loving. It is a lovely healing powder made of ambrosia, calming every illness born of worldly existence. Like Śiva’s pure sacred ash, it gives beauty, auspiciousness and joy; applied as a tilak, it cleans the mirror of the mind and brings every virtue under one’s sway. The jewel-like radiance of the teacher’s toenails awakens divine sight, dispels the darkness of delusion, opens the pure inner eyes and ends the faults and sorrows of worldly night. Then the hidden and manifest jewels of Rāma’s deeds become visible in every mine. As a skilled seeker applies sacred collyrium and wondrously sees abundant treasures in mountain, forest and earth, so does this grace reveal them.

With the soft, lovely dust of the teacher’s feet as collyrium, I cleanse the eyes of discernment and describe Rāma’s liberating deeds. I first bow to the feet of the earth-gods, the Brahmins, who remove doubt born of delusion, and lovingly salute the virtuous assembly, treasury of every excellence. A saint’s conduct is like cotton: tasteless, pure and full of virtue; it suffers while concealing others’ faults and therefore wins honour throughout the world. The joyful fellowship of saints is a moving Prayāga: devotion to Rāma is its Gaṅgā, contemplation of Brahman its Sarasvatī, prescribed action that removes the age’s impurity its Yamunā, and the stories of Hari and Hara its confluence. Firm trust in one’s dharma is its sacred fig tree and good deeds its pilgrims. Available everywhere and always, it removes distress and immediately grants its evident fruit: those who hear, understand and bathe in it with love receive the four aims of life while still embodied.

See the fruit of bathing in holy company at once: crows become cuckoos and cranes become swans. Do not marvel, for the greatness of fellowship with saints is no secret; Vālmīki, Nārada and pot-born Agastya each testified to what it did for them. Every aquatic, terrestrial, aerial, inert or conscious being that has gained understanding, fame, salvation, prosperity or goodness did so through such fellowship; neither ordinary experience nor the Veda knows another means. Discernment does not arise without holy company, and holy company is not easily gained without Rāma’s grace. It is the root of joy and auspiciousness, spiritual practices its flowers and fulfilment its fruit. The wicked improve through it as base metal through the philosopher’s stone; the good, even in bad company, preserve their nature like the gem on a serpent’s head. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva and learned poets speak of saints with diffidence; how could I, a vegetable seller asked to appraise jewels, describe them? I bow to saints, even-minded toward friend and foe, like flowers held between two palms that equally perfume both hands. Hearing this childlike plea, may they graciously grant love for Rāma’s feet.

I now sincerely bow even to the wicked, who without cause oppose everyone. They profit from another’s loss and grieve at another’s flourishing. They eclipse the fame of Hari and Hara like Rāhu eclipses the full moon and champion harmful acts like Sahasrabāhu; thousand-eyed for others’ faults, they are flies in the ghee of others’ welfare. Their heat is fire, anger Yama’s buffalo, and their wealth consists of sins and defects. Like a comet they arise for universal harm, yet sleep as soundly as Kumbhakarṇa. They discard even their bodies to ruin another’s work, like hailstones that melt after destroying crops. I bow to them as wrathful Śeṣa with a thousand mouths for recounting faults, as king Pṛthu with ten thousand ears for hearing sins, and as Indra with thunderbolt speech and a thousand eyes ever fixed on faults. Such is the wicked nature: they burn on hearing the welfare of stranger, enemy or friend. Knowing this, I join both hands and lovingly petition them.

I have made my appeal from my side; may the wicked not turn their attention toward me. Even a crow raised with great love never becomes vegetarian. I bow to the feet of saints and of the unvirtuous: both cause pain, though differently—the former take one’s life-breath when they depart, the latter inflict terrible pain when they arrive. Both arise together in the world yet differ in nature, like lotus and leech born in the same water. Saints and the wicked resemble nectar and wine, though both have the same fathomless ocean-world as parent. Each gains fame or infamy according to conduct. Nectar, moon, Gaṅgā and saints are beneficent; poison, fire, the river of this age’s impurity and disease are destructive. Everyone knows virtue and fault, but each finds pleasing what accords with one’s disposition. The good embrace goodness and the base baseness; nectar is praised for immortality and poison for death.

The sins and faults of the wicked and the virtues of saints are unfathomable oceans; after entering both, I have described only a little, for one cannot choose or reject without first discerning. The Creator brought good and bad into being in every way, while the Vedas distinguished them by counting their qualities and faults. Vedas, histories and Purāṇas say that the Creator’s manifold world is mingled with paired opposites: pain and pleasure, sin and merit, day and night, saint and sinner, good and bad birth, demon and god, high and low, nectar and poison, life and death, māyā and Brahman, soul and Lord, wealth and poverty, pauper and king, Kāśī and Magadha, Gaṅgā and Karmanāśā, barren Marwar and fertile Mālava, Brahmin and cow-killer, heaven and hell, attachment and detachment. The scriptures divide these qualities and faults. The Creator made the animate and inanimate world full of both; saintly swans take the milk of virtue and leave the water of defect.

When the Creator grants such discernment, the mind abandons faults and delights in virtues. Through time, temperament, action or compelling circumstance, even good people may lapse under nature’s power; devotees of Hari correct them, crushing sorrow and fault and giving stainless honour. The wicked may do good in noble company, yet their ingrained impurity does not disappear. Deceivers in fine dress receive honour through the dress, but their end exposes them, as with Kālanemi, Rāvaṇa and Rāhu. Conversely, even in poor dress saints are honoured, as Jāmbavān and Hanumān were. Bad company is loss and good company gain: world and Veda alike attest this. Dust rises to the sky with wind but becomes mud with lowly water. Parrots and mynahs in saints’ or sinners’ homes respectively remember Rāma or pour out abuse. Smoke with bad company becomes soot for the Purāṇas’ ink; joined with fire, wind and water it becomes a life-giving cloud. Planets, medicines, water, wind and cloth become harmful or helpful through bad or good conjunction—perceptive people see this. Bright and dark fortnights have the same light and darkness, but the moon nourishes in one and wanes in the other, so the world grants fame and blame. Knowing every animate and inanimate being to be filled with Rāma, I bow to all their lotus feet; gods, demons, humans, nāgas, birds, spirits, ancestors, gandharvas, kinnaras and night-roamers—may all now show grace.

There are 8.4 million forms and kinds of life dwelling in water, land and sky. Knowing the whole world to be filled with Sītā and Rāma, I join both hands and bow. Recognize me, compassionate ones, as your servant, and together relinquish deceit and favour me. I have no confidence in my own intellect or strength, so I petition everyone. I wish to sing Raghupati’s virtues, but my small mind cannot fathom his deeds; I see not even one effective approach. My mind is poor while its ambition is royal; my understanding is low but its aspiration high. It asks for nectar when the world cannot supply even buttermilk. The good will forgive my boldness and attend to this childlike speech, as parents gladly hear a child’s lisping words. Cruel, crooked fault-finders will laugh, for they wear others’ defects as ornaments. Everyone likes their own poetry, whether rich or insipid; rare indeed are excellent people who rejoice on hearing another’s composition. Many are like ponds and rivers that swell only with their own water, while a rare saint is like the sea, swelling when the full moon rises. My fortune is small and aspiration great, yet I trust that good people will find joy in hearing and the wicked will mock.
